lead: This unit explains how surveyors fix points on the ground and represent them on paper or in a computer. You will learn the principles, the error language, scales and maps, datums, and the two workhorses of distance: tape and EDM. After it you can choose a survey class, read a topographic sheet, apply tape corrections, and compute an EDM distance with its uncertainty.
about: This unit builds the foundation for all surveying: what surveying is, how measurements are made, and how they are placed on a map. Chapter 1.1 classifies surveys and separates plane from geodetic work. Chapter 1.2 explains errors, accuracy and precision, the vocabulary for judging every measurement. Chapter 1.3 turns ground distances into map scales and topographic sheets. Chapter 1.4 fixes the reference surfaces and coordinate systems behind those maps. Chapter 1.5 applies direct measurement with chain and tape, including corrections. Chapter 1.6 introduces electronic distance measurement, the step from tape to total station.

chapters.idea: Surveying determines relative positions of points on or near the earth and represents them on a map; surveys are classified by purpose, instrument and by whether earth curvature matters.
chapters.depth: Define surveying, object and primary principles: work from the whole to the part, and fix a point by at least two independent measurements. Classify by purpose: topographic, cadastral, engineering, control, hydrographic, astronomical. Classify by instrument: chain, compass, theodolite, total station, GNSS. Explain plane surveying: earth treated as flat, area up to about 250 km², most engineering works. Explain geodetic surveying: curvature included, large areas, spheroid, precise control. Mention modern classes UAV and LiDAR only as names; detail is in Unit 5.

figure.aria: A classification tree for surveying, splitting into plane, geodetic, by purpose and by instrument.

chapters.example: A town area is 12 km × 8 km. (a) Is a plane survey acceptable? (b) For a 600 km long geodetic baseline, which survey is needed? (c) Estimate the curvature correction for a 10 km sight with R = 6371 km. (a) Area = 96 km², below about 250 km², so plane surveying is acceptable. (b) 600 km needs geodetic surveying. (c) c = d²/(2R) = (10,000 m)²/(2 × 6,371,000 m) = 7.85 m.
chapters.trap: Do not call every small survey plane and every large survey geodetic without checking the area and precision; the 250 km² limit is a guide, not a law. Also do not reverse the principle: work from the whole to the part, not from the part to the whole.
chapters.leave: Compass, plane table, theodolite and total station details to Units 2, 4 and 5. GNSS, UAV and LiDAR detail to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Every measurement has error; accuracy is closeness to the true value, precision is repeatability, and errors are gross, systematic or random.
chapters.depth: Define true value, observed value, error = observed − true, correction = −error. Explain gross errors, systematic errors (instrumental, personal, natural) and random errors. Distinguish accuracy and precision with simple target or repeated-reading examples. Cover significant figures, mean, deviation, standard deviation and simple propagation for sums and products. Keep least-squares adjustment only as a name; detail is in Unit 4. Use the language of bias and scatter, not advanced statistics.

figure.aria: A tree grouping survey errors into gross, systematic and random, with systematic split into instrumental, personal and natural.

chapters.example: A distance is measured five times: 100.02, 100.04, 100.03, 100.05 and 100.01 m. The true value is 100.00 m. Find the mean, the error of the mean and the sample standard deviation. Mean = 500.15/5 = 100.03 m. Error of mean = 100.03 − 100.00 = +0.03 m. Deviations from mean: −0.01, +0.01, 0.00, +0.02, −0.02 m. Sum of squares = 0.0010 m². Sample variance = 0.0010/4 = 0.00025 m². Standard deviation = 0.016 m.
chapters.trap: Correction has the opposite sign to error. A precise set of readings can still be inaccurate if a systematic bias is present; do not treat low scatter as proof of correctness.
chapters.leave: Weighted adjustment, least squares and error propagation in networks to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A map is a scaled drawing; scale is the ratio of map distance to ground distance, and topographic sheets carry enough marginal information to read the ground.
chapters.depth: Define scale as representative fraction, RF = map distance / ground distance. Cover plain, diagonal, vernier and graphical scales; large and small scale maps. Explain map numbering and marginal information on topographic sheets: title, scale, contour interval, grid reference, north direction. Show unit conversion between cm on map and km on ground. Keep contour interpretation to Unit 3; here only name contours as a map layer.

figure.aria: A tree of map scale types: plain, diagonal, vernier and graphical.

chapters.example: On a map with RF 1:25,000, two points are 6.4 cm apart. Find the ground distance. If a road is 3.5 km long on the ground, find its length on the map. Ground distance = 6.4 cm × 25,000 = 160,000 cm = 1.6 km. Map length = 3.5 km / 25,000 = 350,000 cm / 25,000 = 14 cm.
chapters.trap: Keep the units consistent. An RF has no units; 1:25,000 means 1 cm on the map equals 25,000 cm or 250 m on the ground. Do not write 1 cm = 25,000 m.
chapters.leave: Contours, contour interval and contour interpolation to Unit 3. Map projections to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: A datum fixes the reference surface and origin for coordinates; without a datum, latitude, longitude and height have no precise meaning.
chapters.depth: Define geoid, ellipsoid, horizontal datum and vertical datum. Explain mean sea level, benchmark and orthometric height. Name WGS84 and a local Indian datum only as examples; do not invent transformation parameters. Cover geographic coordinates (latitude, longitude), projected coordinates such as UTM, and Cartesian coordinates. Explain the relation H = h − N, where h is ellipsoidal height, H is orthometric height and N is geoid undulation. Mention datum transformation only as a step when mixing sources.

figure.aria: A stack from earth surface through geoid, ellipsoid, datum and coordinates, showing increasing abstraction.

chapters.example: A GNSS receiver gives ellipsoidal height h = 52.3 m. The geoid undulation at the point is N = −82.0 m. Find the orthometric height H. Also, a point has WGS84 latitude 13.08° N and longitude 80.27° E; name the coordinate system type. H = h − N = 52.3 − (−82.0) = 134.3 m. The coordinates are geographic coordinates.
chapters.trap: Watch the sign of N. A negative geoid undulation makes the orthometric height larger than the ellipsoidal height. Never mix heights from different datums without conversion.
chapters.leave: Map projections and GIS coordinate systems to Unit 7. GPS positioning methods and satellite geometry to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Chain and tape surveying measures distances directly and builds a framework of survey lines with offsets; corrections turn the tape reading into a true distance.
chapters.depth: Describe chain, tape, ranging rods, arrows, cross-staff and optical square. Explain ranging on level and sloping ground, base line, tie line and check line. Cover perpendicular and oblique offsets, field book booking, and obstacles in chaining only briefly. Apply tape corrections: standardization, temperature, tension, sag, slope and alignment. Use correction = measured − true with signs. Keep compass and traverse adjustment to Unit 2.

figure.title: Chain and tape field procedure
figure.aria: A left-to-right flow of chain surveying: reconnaissance, base line, framework, offsets and booking.

chapters.example: A 30 m tape standardized at 20 °C is used at 35 °C to measure 30.000 m. Coefficient of thermal expansion = 11.2 × 10⁻⁶ /°C. Find the temperature correction. A slope measurement is 20.000 m with elevation difference 1.200 m; find the horizontal distance. Temperature correction = L × α × ΔT = 30 × 11.2 × 10⁻⁶ × 15 = 0.00504 m = +5.0 mm. Horizontal distance = √(20.000² − 1.200²) = √398.56 = 19.964 m. Slope correction = −0.036 m.
chapters.trap: Use the measured length, not always the nominal tape length, in temperature and sag corrections. A positive temperature correction means the tape expanded and the recorded distance is too short; add the correction to the measured value.
chapters.leave: Compass surveying, local attraction, latitudes and departures, and traverse adjustment to Unit 2. Levelling and contouring to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: EDM measures distance by sending an electromagnetic wave to a target and comparing phase or travel time; its accuracy is quoted as a constant plus a part per million of the distance.
chapters.depth: Explain pulse and phase-difference EDM. Describe instrument characteristics: range, resolution, accuracy such as ±(3 mm + 3 ppm). Cover accessories: prism, reflectorless target, tribrach, thermometer and barometer. Explain operation and the main errors: prism constant, atmospheric temperature and pressure, cyclic error, instrument and target centring. Mention EDM without reflecting prisms for short ranges. Show the total station only as EDM plus angle measurement; its parts and detailed errors are in Unit 5.

figure.title: EDM phase measurement
figure.aria: A block flow for EDM: transmitter sends a wave to a prism, the receiver collects the return, a phase meter compares it and a distance is computed.

chapters.example: An EDM has accuracy ±(3 mm + 3 ppm). It measures 850.000 m. Find the expected error and express the distance with uncertainty. Distance part = 3 ppm × 850 m = 3 × 10⁻⁶ × 850,000 mm = 2.55 mm. Total error = 3 mm + 2.55 mm = 5.55 mm ≈ 5.6 mm. Distance = 850.000 m ± 0.006 m.
chapters.trap: ppm means parts per million of the measured distance, not millimetres per metre. The constant part and the distance-dependent part are added; do not multiply 3 ppm by the constant 3 mm.
chapters.leave: Total station components, working principle and detailed total station errors to Unit 5. GNSS and satellite positioning to Unit 5.
